entities.summary:
The New Yorker, founded in 1925 in New York City, is an influential American weekly magazine that has profoundly shaped modern journalism, culture, and public discourse. Established by Harold Ross and Jane Grant, it originally aimed to provide a sophisticated and humorous take on urban life, art, and politics, distinguishing itself from other periodicals of the era. Its unique blend of reporting, criticism, and fiction has made it an essential voice in the cultural landscape of the United States, attracting contributions from prominent writers such as E.B. White, John Updike, and Joan Didion, and thereby creating a platform for literary and artistic expression that resonates globally.

Over the decades, The New Yorker has covered pivotal events and cultural shifts, from the Great Depression to the Civil Rights Movement, and more recently, the digital revolution. It launched the careers of countless writers and cartoonists, utilizing its platform to address social issues and comment on political affairs with a distinctive blend of wit and insight. The magazine’s annual festival and its iconic cartoons have become integral to its identity, fostering a loyal readership and influencing popular culture.

The legacy of The New Yorker extends far beyond its pages; it has defined the standards of literary journalism, elevating the profile of magazine writing and inspiring countless periodicals worldwide. Its commitment to high-quality reporting and storytelling has transformed public expectations of journalistic integrity and creativity. As the media landscape continues to evolve, The New Yorker remains a key player, adapting to new technologies while maintaining its core values of cultural critique and literary excellence.
